articles.title: Washington’s new gun permit system moves ahead as one sheriff calls law ‘insane’
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - Washington’s new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms is moving from the statehouse to implementation, with the Washington State...
articles.body:
Washington is implementing a new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms, with the State Patrol building the system that will require state approval before buying a gun.

The permit requirement, effective May 1, 2027, will include fingerprints, proof of training, and a $126 application fee, with renewals costing $90 if submitted before expiration.

Franklin County Sheriff Jim Raymond criticizes the law as unconstitutional, arguing that it places an additional layer of government approval on law-abiding citizens who have already passed background checks.

(The Center Square) - Washington's new permit-to-purchase requirement for firearms is moving from the statehouse to implementation, with the Washington State Patrol now building the system that will require firearm buyers to obtain state approval before purchasing a gun.

The permit requirement does not take effect until May 1, 2027, but work is already underway on the technology and processes needed to launch the program.

The agency says it is targeting early 2027 for the permit application and firearms-training certification systems so applicants have time to obtain permits before the law becomes mandatory.

That development is drawing renewed criticism from Franklin County Sheriff Jim Raymond, who says the law goes too far and could ultimately face a constitutional challenge.

"I think this is insane," Raymond said in a phone interview Wednesday with The Center Square.

Raymond said he believes the new permit requirement is unconstitutional because law-abiding Americans already have a constitutional right to keep and bear arms.

His criticism centers on what he sees as another layer of government approval for people who have already passed existing background checks.

"It's another level of control," Raymond said.

The permit application itself will include fingerprints, proof of the required training and an application fee. The law allows the State Patrol to charge fees intended to cover the direct and indirect costs of administering the permit program. The Legislature's bill report outlines the permit's five-year validity and fee structure.

The new permit-to-purchase application will cost $126 — a $90 permit fee plus a $36 fingerprint-processing fee. Local law enforcement agencies may also charge an additional fee to collect fingerprints. The permit will be valid for five years.

Renewals will cost $90 if submitted before the permit expires. A renewal filed within 90 days after expiration will cost an additional $25 late fee.

Under RCW 9.41.121 , which stemmed from House Bill 1163 that was signed by Gov. Bob Ferguson on May 20, 2025, Washington residents will have to obtain a five-year permit before purchasing or transferring a firearm beginning May 1, 2027.

"Gun violence in Washington state breaks apart too many families and kills too many children," Ferguson said after the signing . "We must put commonsense reforms into place that save lives."

The legislation was championed by gun safety organizations such as the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.

"Washington's new law reflects the commitment of local advocates to a public health approach to gun violence prevention," said Kelly Roskam, director of law and policy at the Center, in a statement after the signing. "Firearm Purchaser Licensing is one of the most effective tools we have for reducing gun deaths."

Applicants will have to submit fingerprints through their local law enforcement agency, have completed a certified firearms safety training course within the previous five years, and pay the required fees. Washington law spells out the application and fingerprint requirements.

The new permit system will operate in addition to Washington's existing firearm background-check requirements and waiting period.

Raymond questioned why the state needs another process for people who are already legally eligible to own firearms.

"It's hard to respond to some of these stupid laws they try to pass nowadays," Raymond said.

He argued that criminals who are already willing to break the law are unlikely to be deterred by another permitting requirement.

"People that aren't law-abiding are going to figure out other ways to purchase firearms," Raymond said.

Raymond said he believes the policy places the burden primarily on law-abiding gun owners rather than addressing people who use firearms to commit crimes.

"People cause problems, not weapons themselves," he said.

The sheriff said he has supported some firearm-safety efforts, including classes offered through his own office. But he views the permit-to-purchase requirement differently.

Raymond said his concern is not limited to the training requirement. Instead, he objects to requiring someone to obtain government permission before making a purchase that he believes is protected by the Constitution.

The law could face scrutiny over its Second Amendment implications. The U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen established a historical-tradition framework for evaluating firearm regulations.

For now, Washington is moving forward with implementation. There are no current legal challenges to RCW 9.41.121 in the courts.

Beginning May 1, state law will prohibit a dealer from delivering a firearm unless the purchaser has a valid permit, has been cleared through the state background-check program and has satisfied the applicable waiting-period requirements.

Raymond, who has only a few months remaining in office, said his opposition to the law will not change his department's responsibility to enforce the law while continuing to defend constitutional rights.

He said the Franklin County Sheriff's Office will continue doing what it can to protect the rights of residents.

"All law enforcement believe in the Constitution and hold to it," Raymond said.

articles.title: Lula x Flávio Bolsonaro: Datafolha aponta empate técnico no 1º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta (17) aponta empate técnico entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro. Levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S. Paulo.
articles.summary: Diferença entre eles está dentro do intervalo da margem de erro da pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17).
articles.body:
Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) estão tecnicamente empatados na disputa pela presidência no 1º turno, segundo pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17), a duas semanas da votação.

Lula tem 39% das intenções de voto, mesmo índice registrado na semana passada.

Flávio aparece com 36% , após oscilar um ponto para cima (tinha 35%).

A diferença de três pontos está dentro do intervalo da margem de erro, que é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. Entenda o que é margem de erro .

Em agosto, Lula tinha seis pontos de vantagem para Flávio Bolsonaro.

Há empate técnico também no 2º turno : 46% para Lula e 44% para Flávio.

Os dois candidatos empatam no índice de rejeição : 47% para cada um.

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo.

Veja os números da pesquisa estimulada do 1º turno , em que o Datafolha mostra aos eleitores os nomes dos candidatos. Entre parênteses, o resultado da pesquisa anterior, do dia 11 de setembro .

Datafolha, 1º turno: intenção de voto (estimulada) — Foto: Arte/g1

Escritor Augusto Cury (Avante): 6% (eram 6%)

Veterinário Wilson Grassi (Democrata): 0 (era zero)

O Datafolha ouviu 2.002 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 15 e 16 de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro no TSE é BR-04029/2026.

Nos votos válidos , quando o Datafolha exclui votos em branco, nulos e indecisos, Lula tem 43% e Flávio, 39%.

Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos e Romeu Zema — Foto: Globo

O Datafolha mostra também que 76% dos eleitores estão totalmente decididos sobre a escolha do candidato a presidente, e que 24% ainda podem mudar o voto. Entre os eleitores de Lula, 84% já estão decididos. Esse índice é de 82% no grupo que declara voto em Flávio Bolsonaro.

Veja agora os números da pesquisa espontânea , em que o Datafolha não mostra os nomes dos candidatos aos eleitores. A parcela de indecisos encolheu de 32% para 21% desde agosto.

Datafolha, 1º turno: intenção de voto (espontânea) — Foto: Arte/g1

Escritor Augusto Cury (Avante): 3% (eram 3%)

O Datafolha perguntou aos eleitores em quem eles não votariam de jeito nenhum no 1º turno. Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro empatam também na rejeição .

Datafolha: rejeição dos candidatos a presidente no 1º turno — Foto: Arte/g1

Escritor Augusto Cury (Avante): 9% (eram 10%)

Veterinário Wilson Grassi (Democrata): 6% (eram 7%)

Votaria em qualquer um/não rejeita nenhum: 2% (era 2%)

Rejeita todos/não votaria em nenhum: 2% (era 2%)

Os números da disputa entre Lula e Flávio no 2º turno, são os mesmos das duas pesquisas anteriores. Ou seja, há estabilidade nesse cenário.

Em outra simulação, Augusto Cury chega a 44% e empata numericamente com Lula, que também tem 44%.

Datafolha, 2º turno: Lula x Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Arte/g1

Datafolha, 2º turno: Lula x Cury — Foto: Arte/g1

Datafolha, 2º turno: Lula x Caiado — Foto: Arte/g1

Datafolha, 2º turno: Lula x Zema — Foto: Arte/g1

Datafolha, 2º turno: Lula x Renan Santos — Foto: Arte/g1

A pesquisa mostra estabilidade também nos índices de aprovação e desaprovação do governo.

Desaprova: 50% (eram 50% na pesquisa anterior)

Quanto à avaliação, 42% consideram o governo ruim ou péssimo e 34% dizem que é ótimo ou bom. Para 23%, é regular.

No mesmo momento do mandato (3 anos e 8 meses), o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro tinha 42% de ruim/péssimo, 30% de ótimo/bom e 25% de regular.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: Omar Aziz participa de sabatina e afirma que vai construir sete hospitais no interior do estado | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas apresentou propostas para a saúde pública no estado.
articles.summary: Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas apresentou propostas para a saúde pública no estado.
articles.body:
Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz participou de sabatina promovida por portais de notícia em Manaus. — Foto: Reprodução/Amazonas Atual

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz ( PSD ), participou de uma sabatina promovida por um conglomerado de portais de noticiais, em Manaus . Durante o compromisso, nesta quinta-feira (17), prometeu a construção de hospitais de alta e média complexidade no interior do estado.

Omar Aziz disputa o cargo pela coligação "Força Amazonas", formada pelo Partido Social Democrático (PSD), Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB) e Republicanos. O candidato já foi governador do estado entre 2010 e 2014 e, posteriormente, foi eleito senador e reeleito ao cargo em 2022.

Questionado sobre projetos voltados à saúde, Omar criticou a falta de novos hospitais construídos no estado pelas gestões anteriores. Ele prometeu a criação de novas maternidades na capital e sete hospitais regionais em municípios estratégicos.

"O último hospital construído no Amazonas foi eu como governador. O último. De lá pra cá não construiram mais nenhum. Em Manaus, nós precisamos fazer três maternidades urgentes. [...] Eu tenho que fazer sete hospitais regionais de alta e média complexidade no interior. É inadmissível uma cidade como Itacoatiara não ter um hospital para que pegue aquela região do baixo Amazonas. Em Parintins, por exemplo, nós vamos fazer um hospital regional de 150 leitos", afirmou.

A agenda do candidato continuou pela tarde com viagem a município da Região Metropolitana de Manaus, onde participa de evento popular durante a noite.

A campanha eleitoral começou no dia 16 de agosto em todo o país. Os candidatos já podem fazer propaganda nas ruas e na internet. Na TV e no rádio, a propaganda começou no dia 28 de agosto. O primeiro turno das eleições será no dia 4 de outubro.

articles.title: Datafolha aponta empate triplo entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento mostra empate técnico entre os dois no 1º e no 2º turno e igualdade numérica nos índices de rejeição. Levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S. Paulo. Margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.
articles.summary: Nova pesquisa Datafolha mostra empate técnico entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no 1º e 2º turno, além de igualdade nos índices de rejeição dos candidatos.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

A duas semanas do 1º turno da eleição, a pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17) aponta um empate triplo entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na disputa pela Presidência da República.

Os dois estão tecnicamente empatados nas intenções de voto no 1º turno e no 2º turno e aparecem numericamente empatados na rejeição . O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo.

Segundo o instituto, Lula (PT) tem 39% das intenções de voto no 1º turno, mesmo percentual registrado na semana passada. Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) tem 36%, contra 35% na pesquisa anterior. Com três pontos de diferença entre os dois e margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos, Lula e Flávio estão tecnicamente empatados.

De acordo com o Datafolha, a distância de três pontos entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no 1º turno é a menor desde a primeira quinzena de maio , quando a diferença também era de três pontos (38% a 35%). Desde então, a diferença chegou a dez pontos em junho e vem diminuindo: foi de oito pontos em julho, seis em agosto, cinco no início de setembro e quatro na semana passada.

Em um cenário de 2º turno entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro , Lula tem 46% das intenções de voto e Flávio, 44%. Os dois repetem os índices registrados no levantamento anterior e mantêm o empate técnico. Brancos, nulos ou nenhum somam 8%, e os indecisos são 1%.

O Datafolha também perguntou aos eleitores em quem eles não votariam de jeito nenhum no 1º turno. Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula estão numericamente empatados, com 47% de rejeição cada. No leva ntamento anterior, ambos tinham 46%.

Veja o detalhamento desses números abaixo.

Escritor Augusto Cury (Avante): 6% (eram 6%)

Veterinário Wilson Grassi (Democrata): 0 (era zero)

Datafolha, 1º turno: intenção de voto (estimulada) — Foto: Arte/g1

Na pesquisa anterior, do dia 11 de setembro , Lula tinha 39%, Flávio Bolsonaro aparecia com 35%. Segundo o instituto, o presidente estava em ligeira vantagem.

O Datafolha ouviu 2.002 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 15 e 16 de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro no TSE é BR-04029/2026.

O Datafolha perguntou aos eleitores em quem eles não votariam de jeito nenhum no 1º turno. Os números:

Escritor Augusto Cury (Avante): 9% (eram 10%)

Veterinário Wilson Grassi (Democrata): 6% (eram 7%)

Votaria em qualquer um/não rejeita nenhum: 2% (era 2%)

articles.title: Datafolha: Lula tem 53% no Bolsa Família e Flávio Bolsonaro, 28% | G1
articles.standfirst: Entre quem não recebe o benefício, Flávio tem 37% das intenções de voto, e Lula, 36%. Margem de erro no segmento é de 5 pontos percentuais.
articles.summary: Datafolha aponta que Lula lidera entre quem recebe Bolsa Família, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro empata tecnicamente no grupo que não possui o benefício social.
articles.body:
Programa Bolsa Família — Foto: Divulgação/MDS

Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17) mostra que, entre quem recebe o Bolsa Família ou mora com um beneficiário, Lula (PT) tem 53% das intenções de voto no primeiro turno, contra 28% de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Entre os que não recebem o benefício nem moram com beneficiários, Flávio Bolsonaro tem 37% e Lula, 36%.

No 2º turno, entre os beneficiários, Lula aparece com 60%, contra 33% de Flávio Bolsonaro.

A pesquisa foi realizada entre 15 e 17 de setembro, em sua maior parte antes do anúncio do reajuste de 15% no Bolsa Família, feito nesta quinta. O piso passará de R$ 600 para R$ 691, com pagamentos a partir de 19 de outubro.

A margem de erro geral é de dois pontos percentuais. Entre quem recebe o benefício ou mora com um beneficiário, é de cinco pontos.

articles.summary: 47% afirmam que não votariam no candidato do PT de jeito nenhum e 47% afirmam que não votariam no candidato do PL.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (17) mostra que Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) são os candidatos à Presidência mais rejeitados, ambos com o mesmo índice: 47% dizem que não votariam no presidente de jeito nenhum e 47% afirmam que não votariam no senador.

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo. Na pesquisa anterior, divulgada em 11 de setembro, também havia empate, com 46% de rejeição para cada um .

Os demais candidatos estão em um patamar menor de rejeição: Renan Santos (Missão) tem 15%; Romeu Zema (Novo), 14%; Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), 13%; e Rui Costa Pimenta (PCO), 11%.

Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert e Vittor Sales

No 2º turno, o presidente aparece com 46%, contra 44% do senador . Os números se repetem desde o começo do mês na série de pesquisas do Datafolha.

articles.title: Araceli Lemos propõe cobrar devedores fiscais  | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Estado participou de encontro com representantes de movimentos de mulheres em Belém nesta quinta-feira, 17.
articles.summary: Candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Estado cumpriu agenda de campanha com representantes de movimentos de mulheres em Belém, nesta quinta-feira, 17.
articles.body:
A candidata do PSOL ao Governo do Pará, Araceli Lemos, disse nesta quinta-feira (17) que pretende cobrar débitos fiscais de grandes empresas para criar um fundo destinado a financiar educação, inovação e geração de renda, com prioridade para mulheres chefes de família.

"Nós vamos fazer com que aqueles que não estão pagando paguem o que devem para que o estado tenha mais recursos", afirmou.

Araceli participou de um encontro na sede do Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL), no bairro de São Brás, em Belém, para debater a rede de proteção às mulheres. Acompanhada da candidata a vice-governadora, Fátima Santana, ela apresentou propostas do plano de governo a representantes de movimentos de mulheres da capital.

Durante a agenda, a candidata defendeu o combate ao feminicídio, a instalação de delegacias especializadas com funcionamento 24 horas em todos os municípios do estado e a implantação de um programa de prevenção à violência contra a mulher.

Para financiar as propostas, Araceli afirmou que pretende cobrar dívidas tributárias, fazer uma auditoria nas isenções fiscais e reduzir despesas que a campanha considera excessivas. A candidata citou especialmente grandes empresas dos setores mineral e do agronegócio.

Segundo Araceli, um levantamento usado pela campanha aponta que uma única empresa teria cerca de R$ 2 bilhões em débitos com o estado. Ela não identificou a empresa durante a agenda.

"Nós vamos fazer uma verdadeira auditoria nas isenções fiscais, porque nós achamos importantes as isenções para aqueles que geram emprego e que pagam seus impostos", declarou.

A candidata estima obter cerca de R$ 10 bilhões a partir de diferentes medidas. Além da cobrança de débitos e da revisão de isenções, ela citou redução de gastos com publicidade e eventos e valores que, segundo a campanha, estariam relacionados a obras superfaturadas.

Araceli não detalhou como chegou à estimativa de R$ 10 bilhões.

"Nós temos condições de arrecadar valores aproximados a R$ 10 bilhões para estar investindo em melhoria das condições das mulheres no estado do Pará", afirmou.

Questionada sobre a criação do fundo, Araceli disse que a medida dependerá de aprovação da Assembleia Legislativa do Pará (Alepa). Segundo a candidata, uma proposta semelhante apresentada por ela quando era deputada estadual foi rejeitada.

"Agora será um projeto do Executivo para a Assembleia Legislativa", disse.

articles.title: Homem é preso após esfaquear pai para defender cadela de agressões | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso ocorreu nesta quinta-feira (17) em Presidente Prudente. Policiais encontraram a cadela machucada e a faca usada no crime quebrada; idoso internado no HR pediu proteção à Justiça.
articles.summary: Um homem de 29 anos foi preso em flagrante nesta quinta-feira (17) em Presidente Prudente (SP). Ele é suspeito de esfaquear o pai para defender sua cadela.
articles.body:
Homem é preso suspeito de tentativa de homicídio após agredir o pai por causa de cadela em Prudente — Foto: Reprodução/Polícia Civil

Um homem de 29 anos foi preso em flagrante suspeito de esfaquear o pai, de 67 anos, para defender sua cadela de estimação de agressões nesta quinta-feira (17), em Presidente Prudente (SP). O crime ocorreu em uma residência no Conjunto Habitacional Augusto de Paula.

Ao chegarem ao local da ocorrência, os policiais militares constataram que o animal estava ferido e apreenderam uma faca quebrada usada no ataque. Em depoimento, o jovem admitiu ter golpeado o pai com o objeto cortante para cessar as agressões contra o animal.

A vítima foi socorrida, levada para o Hospital Regional e pediu uma medida protetiva contra o filho. O estado de saúde não foi divulgado.

O caso foi registrado na Delegacia de Plantão de Presidente Prudente como tentativa de homicídio por motivo fútil. A cadela recebeu socorro por apresentar ferimentos, mas não há novas atualizações sobre o seu estado de saúde.

articles.title: Mendonça rejeita ação que questionava reajuste do Bolsa Família sem analisar legalidade da medida | G1
articles.standfirst: Com o reajuste anunciado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na manhã desta quinta-feira (15), o piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691. O novo valor começa a ser pago no dia 19 de outubro.
articles.summary: Com o reajuste anunciado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na manhã desta quinta-feira (15), o piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691. O novo valor começa a ser pago no dia 19 de outubro.
articles.body:
O ministro André Mendonça , do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), rejeitou uma ação em que o deputado federal e candidato à reeleição Zé Trovão (PL-SC), aliado do senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), questionava o reajuste do Bolsa Família anunciado nesta quinta-feira (15) pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

Mendonça, sorteado relator do caso no TSE, mencionou decisões anteriores segundo as quais um candidato a deputado federal não tem legitimidade para apresentar uma ação contra um candidato à Presidência da República, uma vez que os dois cargos são disputados em circunscrições eleitorais diferentes.

"Ressalto que o reconhecimento da ilegitimidade ativa não importa pronunciamento acerca da legalidade ou da constitucionalidade do reajuste do Programa Bolsa Família, tampouco acerca de sua eventual subsunção ao art. 73, § 10, da Lei nº 9.504/1997", diz Mendonça na decisão desta quinta.

Na ação, o deputado havia afirmado ser "necessária a intervenção da Justiça Eleitoral" para impedir que a estrutura administrativa e os recursos públicos fossem usados de modo a "comprometer a igualdade de oportunidades entre os candidatos."

Zé Trovão havia pedido também que Mendonça determinasse ao governo, de forma provisória (liminar), o não reajuste do benefício até o julgamento da ação ou até o final das eleições.

Com o reajuste anunciado na manhã desta quinta, o piso do programa passa de R$ 600 para R$ 691. O novo valor começa a valer no mês de outubro, com pagamentos a partir do dia 19, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno (se houver) das eleições presidenciais.

Segundo o Ministério do Planejamento, o custo do reajuste do Bolsa Família neste ano será de R$ 5,8 bilhões. Para 2027, o impacto nas despesas será de R$ 22,7 bilhões.

O Ministério da Fazenda informou que o reajuste do Bolsa Família apenas repõe as perdas inflacionárias dos últimos anos, o que não equivaleria a um aumento do benefício social.

O ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, negou que a medida tenha relação com as eleições de 2026.

De acordo com a Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), a lei que instituiu o novo Bolsa Família, em 2023, autoriza o Poder Executivo a "corrigir os valores dos benefícios e proíbe sua redução".

articles.title: 20 states sue to block Trump admin rule that would make it harder for immigrants to obtain visas, green cards
articles.summary: More than 20 states sued the Department of Homeland Security over a public charge rule that could increase green card denials based on Medicaid and SNAP use.
articles.body:
More than 20 states are suing the Trump administration over a new Department of Homeland Security rule expanding the list of government aid that could disqualify immigrants from obtaining visas or green cards.

The rule, set to take effect on Friday, would allow immigration officials to consider an immigrant's use of benefits like Medicaid and SNAP when determining their likelihood of becoming dependent on government aid.

The states' and cities' lawsuits aim to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it, arguing that the new rule is arbitrary and exceeds the agency's authority.

More than 20 states are suing the Trump administration over a new Department of Homeland Security rule that would give immigration officials wider discretion in determining what constitutes a public charge, a statute that allows the government to deny visas or green cards to applicants it determines are likely to become dependent on government assistance.

The rule, which is set to take effect on Friday, would expand the list of possible government aid that officials could point to when deciding to disqualify an applicant.

New York State Attorney General Letitia James led a coalition of 21 states and Washington, D.C., in suing the administration over what they describe as punishment for immigrants' lawful use of public assistance. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani led a separate lawsuit filed by a coalition of cities challenging DHS' rule.

James said the rule would allow immigration officials to consider an immigrant's use of benefits like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and participation in school meal programs when determining whether they could become dependent on government aid. She also said it could lead to more fear of interacting with the government for people who are part of an immigrant family.

"Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported," James said in a statement. "This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled. My office fought this exact policy once before and won, and we are leading the nation to ensure the Trump administration cannot inflict this harm on families again."

The public charge ground applies to certain immigrants seeking admission or adjustment of status. Most undocumented immigrants are ineligible for federal means-tested public benefits, although limited exceptions exist under federal and state law.

The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants pull from programs over fears about the public charge rule.

Immigration officials under the Biden administration's 2022 public charge rule generally considered only cash assistance for income maintenance, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), along with government-funded long-term institutionalization, when determining a public charge.

The rule does not specify a fixed list of public benefits that immigration officials may consider. Instead, it states that officers may consider the receipt of any means-tested public benefits as part of a public charge determination, giving them broader discretion in evaluating applicants.

The states' and cities' lawsuits asked the courts to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it.

"It's very hard to predict how courts will look at this issue. It is very unusual regulation though," Cato Institute Director of Immigration Studies David Bier told Fox News Digital. "I think from that standpoint, the states have a good argument that we had a well-defined public charge rule and the administration didn't replace it with some other well-defined rule, it replaced it with nothing. So now there's just discretion to the officers to do whatever they want with the underlying statute. There's no regulation that clearly says this is what it means to be a public charge in the United States."

"The rule as it was before this new regulation was you had to be primarily dependent on certain government benefit programs. This rule removes that definition and doesn't replace it with anything. So now people and applicants, lawyers who are applying to the government on behalf of applicants, they don't know really what the law is," he continued.

The states' lawsuit argues that DHS is exceeding its authority because Congress did not approve a broader interpretation of what it means to be a public charge. The states say the new rule is arbitrary and that the agency ignored the harmful consequences of the change.

"Cruelty is the point," James said at a press conference on Monday. "Having a chilling effect on immigrants is the point. Letting individuals know that they are not welcome here is the point. Immigration animus is the point. The fact that you're going to deny individuals who are sick and hungry and homeless benefits just is beyond the pale."

DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

Bier said the rule does not prohibit immigrants from receiving welfare and is only used as an officer's projection about someone's likelihood of future welfare use in the U.S., warning that it could lead to self-sufficient applicants being denied.

"Whether someone is currently using benefits or not doesn't matter under this evaluation. It's this probabilistic determination of the future that they're using in order to deny people legal status and legal permanent resident status in the United States. That's a much more difficult assessment to make. That's going to result in arbitrary denials. It's just not possible to do this type of assessment and not result in people who would be self-sufficient being denied status," he said.

This comes as President Donald Trump pursues a broader immigration crackdown that has extended beyond illegal immigration to legal immigration pathways. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on curbing illegal immigration, his administration has also imposed additional restrictions on legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas and new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the U.S.

The administration has also pursued visa revocations and removal proceedings in cases involving political activity and speech, including some anti-Israel activists. Those efforts have prompted court challenges in which plaintiffs allege violations of First Amendment free speech and Fifth Amendment due process protections.

"It's very clear that this administration wants to restrict both illegal immigration, which obviously it's done at the border, and through deportations, but also legal immigration," Bier said.

Last month, the administration directed U.S. embassies and consulates around the world to postpone immigrant visa interviews while consular officers complete training on new public charge guidance, temporarily stalling applications that had reached the interview stage.

"The primary population that's going to be affected by this public charge rule are spouses of U.S. citizens and their kids who are trying to receive green cards so they can live with their American spouse or parent here in the United States. That's the overwhelming majority of the people who are going to be affected by the rule. It's going to result in many of those immigrant families being separated from their American spouse or parent," Bier said.

The public charge provision stems from the Immigration Act of 1882, when federal lawmakers sought to ensure that immigrants would be able to take care of themselves and not become a public burden.

After years of only considering cash benefits, the first Trump administration widened the categories of benefit programs that could be considered a public charge, including Medicaid, food stamps and housing vouchers. But the Biden administration in 2022 published a rule that returned to the previous guidance. The rule set to take effect this week would rescind the Biden administration's rule.

The new rule is broader than the one from the first Trump administration, as it does not specify which safety nets should be considered and only states that DHS "will consider the receipt of any means-tested public benefits."

"One of the most important things to understand is that during the first Trump administration, they had a public charge rule that was well defined that really did explain exactly what you were supposed to do in order to not be deemed a public charge or who was a public charge. This is completely different from that. It's essentially the Wild West. No one knows what's going on; no one knows what the law is now," Bier said.

images.caption: The rule, which is set to take effect on Friday, would expand the list of possible government aid that officials could point to when deciding to disqualify an applicant.
The rule applies only to legal immigrants in the U.S., as illegal immigrants are not eligible for public benefits.
The states' and cities' lawsuits asked the courts to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it.

articles.title: Zuckerberg, Musk And Huang Reportedly Convinced Trump To Block AI Regulator
articles.summary: Zuckerberg and Huang have recently opposed calls to slow down frontier AI development while Musk has backed a push by Amodei to pace advancements until
articles.body:
Billionaire tech CEOs Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang spoke with President Donald Trump last month and convinced him to block efforts to establish an AI industry-funded regulator, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, despite growing fears about AI safety.

Citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter, the Journal reported Meta's Zuckerberg, SpaceXAI's Musk and Nvidia's Huang opposed a push by some AI executives to build an industry-funded oversight body similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

The proposal for a FINRA-style AI regulatory and standards body came from Google's Chief Scientist Demis Hassabis, who also chairs the tech giant's DeepMind AI unit.

The billionaires' purported concern about the proposal stemmed from fears it would entrench more power in the hands of the three leading American AI labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's DeepMind.

All three expressed their concerns to Trump in separate conversations, after which the president didn't move forward with proposals for setting up the regulator.

According to the Journal, administration officials have told top AI executives that building consensus on an AI regulatory framework at the White House is challenging because CEOs opposing such moves are contacting Trump directly.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Huang are expected to attend next week's State Dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping. Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as CEO but remained on the board as the company's government liaison, will also be in attendance. Despite Trump's recent dismissal of AI safety fears and push to beat China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios that the Trump administration is "open to discussions on avoiding shared risks" on the issue.

What Has Zuckerberg Said About AI Safety Recently?

On Tuesday, both Zuckerberg and Huang downplayed concerns about AI safety risks and argued that companies can pace themselves without external regulation. Zuckerberg outlined his argument in a lengthy X post , arguing that companies have a "strong natural incentive" to ensure AI is aligned to safety and human interests, as people will not use AI agents that are "misaligned with them and…don't do what they ask." Meta's billionaire CEO also appeared to dismiss the argument that AI companies may need to coordinate to ensure safety, noting that "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens." Zuckerberg, however, said his company was open to engaging independent evaluators and advisers on AI, agreeing with Anthropic and OpenAI.

What Has Huang Said About AI Safety Recently?

Huang also dismissed slowdown talks and safety fears on Tuesday, telling attendees at Salesforce's annual Dreamforce event that the question of having to choose between safety and speed was a "false" one. "You could definitely have both at the same time." He then argued: "We don't need new laws — we don't need new regulations." Huang then pointed to market forces and said companies should pace themselves until they are confident about "releasing something that the market would appreciate." A day earlier, he had attended a call from Trump while he was live on stage during the All-In Summit. In the call, Trump argued that people opposing AI and data center construction were "playing right into the hands" of skeptics and China and declared, "We're not going to let that happen." Huang told the president, "You're right. We're not going to let that happen, sir."

What Has Musk Said About AI Safety Recently?

Last week, Musk questioned and mocked a series of viral X posts made by Jacob Coxon, an ex-Anthropic researcher, who quit the company and raised alarm about AI-driven human extinction over the next decade. Musk said the posts seemed like a 'setup and argued that this was a spark that followed "groundwork" for a "psy op (for lack of a better term)," presumably against AI. But when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued warnings about AI safety and called for "pacing" the development of frontier AI models and better coordination on safety, Musk wrote, " Dario is right ." However, unlike Anthropic and OpenAI, Musk's SpaceXAI has not laid out any plans to coordinate or pace frontier AI model development.

articles.title: Watch Mitch McConnell cast deciding vote on Senate farm bill
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell, who returned to Congress in September after being hospitalized in June, cast the deciding vote to advance a Senate farm bill.
articles.body:
Sen. Mitch McConnell , R-Kentucky, cast a crucial vote for Senate Republicans to advance a farm bill on Sept. 16, days after returning to Congress from a months-long absence.

With McConnell's vote, the Senate Agriculture Committee moved to advance a farm bill , or a massive legislative package that sets national agriculture, nutrition, conservation and forestry policy , out of committee. Despite opposition from Democrats on the committee, the bill advanced 12-11 with Republicans voting along party lines.

The Republican senator returned to the Senate on Sept. 14, capping his prolonged absence after a fall and bout with pneumonia landed him in the hospital.

McConnell's time away from Capitol Hill sparked widespread speculation about his well-being.

"I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues," he said in a Sept. 14 statement before casting an early evening vote, his first since his return.

Republican leader McConnell returns to Senate post-recovery

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 14, 2026, in Washington, DC. This is McConnell’s first public appearance in over 90 days after he recovered from a fall and illness.

Watch Mitch McConnell cast key farm bill vote

McConnell, sitting in a wheelchair, cast his vote on the farm bill on Sept. 16, voting along party lines to give the legislation the push it needed to advance out of committee.

When called on, the 84-year-old appeared to raise his finger, seemingly in favor of the bill. Sen. John Hoeven, R-North Dakota, who was sitting to McConnell's left, then leaned over and appeared to say something to him.

After McConnell's name was called a second time, the senator can be heard saying "aye" in a soft-spoken voice.

Watch the video at the top of this story.

Later, McConnell posted a statement on social media , in part saying he "was proud to vote yes" on the bill.

"My hope is the bill receives robust bipartisan support on the Senate floor and demonstrates our commitment to our Nation's farmers and rural communities," he said.

Though known colloquially as the "farm bill," the legislation is titled The Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026. A sprawling agriculture package, the farm bill is usually passed every five years, though it has not been updated since 2018.

articles.title: White House pulls stalled ICE director nominee
articles.summary: The Oklahoma state trooper had no experience leading a major law enforcement agency but was close to the Homeland Security secretary.
articles.body:
The White House on Thursday withdrew the nomination of Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a Republican blocked his confirmation hearing.

Schroyer's nomination stalled after Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), a foe of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, requested that the Department of Homeland Security provide his committee with more information about its investigation into two ICE and Border Patrol agents accused of killing two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January.

Paul, who as chair controls the committee's hearing and markup agenda, did not oppose Schroyer's nomination, per Drew Carmichael, a spokesperson for the senator.

Schroyer was a surprise pick to lead ICE. He had no experience leading a major law enforcement agency, let alone an organization the size of ICE. But Schroyer has close ties with the DHS secretary. Schroyer at one point led Mullin's security detail and Mullin made Schroyer a senior adviser at DHS.

The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The nomination's withdrawal is a blow to Mullin, who has faced criticism from immigration hardliners over what they have characterized as insufficient progress in achieving mass deportations of unauthorized immigrants from the United States. Mullin had defended his pick to lead ICE, saying he wanted someone who could be confirmed in the Senate.

Mullin's pitch for putting Schroyer in the role in part involved highlighting his experience with helping stand up special units in the Oklahoma Highway Patrol to locate abducted children, as well as his work implementing a state program allowing local police departments to work with ICE on arresting undocumented immigrants.

But immigration hardliners weren't convinced. They and others in the administration doubted Schroyer could lead the complex agency — or even clear the Senate.

Schroyer's abrupt exit means the agency's streak of not having a confirmed leader at the top ranks will continue. The Senate has not confirmed an ICE director since 2014 and there is pessimism within the administration's ranks that the Senate could confirm any nominee with a significant track record at ICE, given how polarizing the agency has become under President Donald Trump.

Acting ICE chief David Venturella, a close ally of White House border czar Tom Homan, has led ICE while Schroyer's nomination was pending. Under federal law, as long as a nominee is pending Venturella can serve in that role indefinitely. Now, the clock starts ticking on a 210 day limit for his tenure, unless someone else is nominated.

Venturella would have his own challenges if he were nominated for the role, including past work for GEO Group, a major private detention company. Some in the administration have said that association would hurt his chances at confirmation to lead ICE in Schroyer's place.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: 71% think Trump administration lacks plan to end Iran war
articles.summary: A Fox News poll finds 70% of voters say Trump lacks a clear strategy for the Iran war, while 60% now call the military action the wrong decision.
articles.body: Nearly seven months into the war with Iran, a new Fox News national survey finds views souring as voters feel the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the war, a growing number think the conflict will make the U.S. less safe and a majority believes the decision to take military action was wrong. Seven in 10 voters think the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, including 95% of Democrats, 83% of independents and 43% of Republicans. In addition, a growing 47% of voters say the conflict will make the U.S. less safe in the long run, up from 39% in April. By comparison, 32% think it will make the country safer, and 20% say there will be no difference. The rise in concern is largest among White voters, voters under 45 and independents. Sixty percent say U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, while 37% say it was right, widening the margin to 23 points, up from 17 points in June (58% to 41%). Attitudes against the war have increased modestly across most demographic groups, with the largest shifts among Hispanic voters, voters under age 30, moderates and voters 65 and over. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE "Typically, the public rallies around the president in response to a foreign policy crisis," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But two things are different here. First, President Trump hasn’t consistently and forcefully made the case for the war, and the U.S. doesn’t have boots on the ground. Both of those things matter for public opinion." FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Trump’s overall job performance stands at 39% approval and 61% disapproval. The president’s ratings on foreign policy are underwater by 24 points. His 37% approval is a second-term low and is just one point above his first-term low of 36% in September 2019. When asked to name the most important issue facing the country, in their own words, only 4% of voters say Iran and a miniscule 1% name foreign policy in general. By comparison, 34% mention the top issue of the cost of living. Meanwhile, by a 10-point margin, more voters say the Democrats are better equipped to handle foreign policy than the Republicans, a reversal from the previous midterm cycle when Republicans were more trusted by 6 points in September 2022. Israel and Ukraine A low of 48% say they side more with the Israelis than the Palestinians (38%) in the ongoing conflict in Gaza. That is down from 54% in June and a high of 68% at the conflict’s outset in October 2023. Since 2023, the sharpest decline in support for Israel — down at least 20 points — comes from women, Hispanic voters, voters under age 45, voters with a college degree and Democrats. Republican support has fallen 10 points during the same time. On Ukraine, voters favor the U.S. continuing to provide financial aid to fight Russia by 16 points (55% to 39%), roughly unchanged during the past two years. Democrats favor supporting Ukraine, while Republicans and independents are divided. One more thing… Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit to the U.S., more than twice as many voters say Trump is not tough enough on China (45%) as say he is too tough (20%). Three in 10 (30%) say his approach is about right. There is bipartisan agreement on this: the largest share of Democrats (44%), Republicans (47%), and independents (44%) say Trump is not tough enough on China. Republicans are more split, with 43% saying his approach is about right. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

articles.title: Unearthed clip exposes what 'DEI Queen' in razor-thin House race thought of 'Back the Blue' law
articles.summary: Christina Bohannan called Iowa's Back the Blue law an "overreaction" to the George Floyd riots, fueling fresh Republican soft-on-crime attacks.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Christina Bohannan, an Iowa state legislator and the Democratic nominee in one of the country’s most competitive districts, once opposed an Iowa Back the Blue law passed in the wake of the 2020 George Floyd riots, calling it an "overreaction." "I think that we’re seeing a backlash and, frankly, an exaggerated backlash, an overreaction to all of that," Bohannan said at a 2021 virtual legislative forum on social justice issues. "That’s what’s happening. A lot of this is happening because they just don’t have a lot of minorities in their districts. They don’t interact with people on any kind of regular basis, and, so, they don’t see these issues." To some onlooking critics, her resurfaced comments are further proof of what they’ve characterized as her soft-on-crime stances, positions they believe are at odds with the electorate of the Hawkeye State as she wages her third campaign to unseat Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa. WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN "Christina Bohannan achieved the ultra rare final boss level of woke where police are bad, criminals are good and anyone who disagrees is racist," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "There is a reason why this DEI queen has been rejected twice by voters. She is straight up nuts, and her soft-on-crime agenda would endanger all Iowans." Bohannan launched her career in education, teaching at the University of Iowa College of Law, where she remained until 2020, when she won a seat in the Iowa House of Representatives, unseating a 20-year Democratic incumbent. Bohannan has run for Congress before. In 2022, she lost to Miller-Meeks in a 53.4% to 46.6% contest. She tried again in 2024 and got closer, losing by a fraction of a percent, 50.0% to 49.8%, and by just 799 votes. VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP In all three races, Republicans have attacked her for her statements as an academic and her voting record as a state legislator, painting her as a soft-on-crime candidate. In the resurfaced clip, Bohannan was referring to Senate File 342, signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in 2021. Among other provisions, the bill raised penalties for rioting, making it a class D felony punishable by five years behind bars, and implemented more stringent punishments for unlawful assembly. The law came amid a wave of anti-police sentiment that swept the country after George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, died after Officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck area during a restraint. The incident sparked widespread debate about law enforcement safety and profiling. Where states like Minnesota and Washington passed restrictions on police and other law enforcement officers, Iowa lawmakers rallied to their support. Iowa Rep. Jarad Klein, a Republican and the bill’s sponsor, framed the legislation as a clear way to support embattled public servants in a floor speech. "Let me be clear: If you support law enforcement, truly support law enforcement, you will be voting ‘yes’ tonight. If you stand up and say you support law enforcement, your words will become meaningless with a ‘no’ vote. Actions speak louder than words," Klein said. Gov. Reynolds echoed that thinking at her signing. "I made it clear in my Condition of the State Address that Iowa’s law enforcement will always have my respect, and I will always have their back. Today’s bill embodies that commitment in a historic way. The public peace is too important, and the safety of our officers too precious to tolerate destructive behavior," Reynolds said in a press release. For her part, Bohannan said she opposed the legislation, arguing it went too far. "The bill that’s coming over to the House from the Senate about the protestors actually would make it OK for a person to drive negligently or grossly negligently and hit a protester, and there would be immunity for that. It’s sick. These are kids, mostly," she said. UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES MORE ANTI-POLICE RHETORIC AS EL-SAYED GETS GRILLED FOR DELETING SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS The final version of the bill does have a provision that protects drivers from civil liability. But it only applies to drivers "exercising due care" and who cause injury to someone engaging in disorderly conduct by blocking traffic on a public street or highway. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bohannan’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital on her statements from 2021 or whether she stood by her views of the Back the Blue bill.

articles.title: Trump's EPA reforms are a huge boost to manufacturers, but there's more red tape to cut: expert
articles.summary: NAM CEO Jay Timmons says Trump EPA rollback of Biden-era power plant emissions standards is a game changer but warns more permitting reform is needed.
articles.body: trump The Trump administration's move to eliminate a swath of Biden-era power plant emissions standards will be a game changer for the U.S. economy, National Association of Manufacturers CEO Jay Timmons told Fox News Digital. Timmons hailed EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for the move announced this week but noted that even more red tape remains to be cut. "It really sent a signal to manufacturers that the administration was listening to our concerns," Timmons said of the cuts to power plant emissions standards. TRUMP'S EPA CHIEF PUSHES BACK ON CLIMATE SKEPTICS BEING LABELED 'SCIENCE DENIERS' He said NAM and other groups had objected to former President Joe Biden's 2024 standards "very, very clearly" at the time, saying the standards were "simply unworkable." "The timeline that they had proposed was just, it wasn't feasible. Not that the aspirations for, you know, for cleaner air and a healthier environment aren't good aspirations," Timmons said. "I think we all share that. I know the current EPA and Administrator Zeldin certainly share those objectives, but how you get there really matters and whether manufacturers are able to meet the challenge. Timmons noted that the Biden administration had heard its concerns but simply disagreed. TRUMP-APPROVED ENERGY PROJECTS AT RISK OF SUDDEN DEATH BY NEXT HOSTILE PRESIDENT The emissions regulations cut this week were removed by executive fiat, but Timmons says more lasting change must come through Congress as manufacturers hope to avoid regulatory whiplash between administrations. "Uncertainty is the absolute worst enemy for manufacturers because manufacturers are on a very long-term horizon when it comes to planning and strategy, product development, research development. So, when administrations change, there has often been kind of that pendulum swing," Timmons said. SEN KEVIN CRAMER: CHINA BUILDS FOR WAR WHILE AMERICA WAITS ON PERMITS One area he said could use further reform is permitting. NAM polling found that 80% of manufacturers say the length and complexity of the permitting process is harmful to increasing investment. As many as 87% of manufacturers told NAM they would expand business operations, hire more workers or increase wages and benefits if the permitting process was more streamlined. SENATE MOVES TO UNSHACKLE AMERICA'S DRIVERS FROM CALIFORNIA'S 'CLIMATE ZEALOTS' Timmons said it is critical for Congress to hear directly from manufacturers when drafting legislation, however. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There needs to be more opportunities for business to be at the table. To really explain what the art of the possible is. No one is saying that we should not be working hard to achieve cleaner air, cleaner water, healthier communities. In fact, we're saying exactly that. We should be part of the solution to make that happen," he said.
